law_name: Constitutional Declaration of the Syrian Arab Republic (الإعلان الدستوري)
description: Signed by al-Sharaa on 13 March 2025 after a committee he appointed on 2 March drafted it, replacing the 2012 constitution for a five-year transitional period. It vests executive power in the president, abolishes the post of prime minister, requires the president to be Muslim, makes Islamic jurisprudence the principal source of legislation, protects freedom of opinion, expression and belief, and creates a People's Assembly (term of 30 months, renewable) two-thirds selected through electoral bodies and one-third appointed by the president. It also provides for transitional justice for crimes of the former government.
significance: The legal framework of the post-Assad state; criticised by Kurdish organisations and by analysts for concentrating power in the presidency (see polemics).

law_name: Decree No. 20 of 2025 establishing the National Commission for Transitional Justice, and companion decree on the National Commission for the Missing
description: Issued on 17 May 2025. The commission, headed by Abdulbaset Abdullatif, has administrative and financial independence and is tasked with uncovering the truth about grave violations by the former government, holding those responsible to account, remedying harm to victims and promoting non-recurrence and national reconciliation. A separate commission was created the same day to investigate the fate of the missing.
significance: First institutional step on transitional justice; Human Rights Watch called its mandate 'troublingly narrow' because it excludes abuses by non-state actors.

law_name: Decrees on the formation of the transitional People's Assembly (June 2025) and Decree No. 143 of 2026 appointing its final third
description: A presidential decree of 13 June 2025 set the rules for forming the Assembly and al-Sharaa appointed its 11-member Higher Committee; the committee raised the size from 150 to 210 seats in July 2025. Electoral colleges chose most of the 140 elective seats in October 2025 and in 2026, and Decree No. 143 of 1 July 2026 appointed the remaining 70 members. The Assembly first met on 12 July 2026.
significance: Created the first legislature since Assad's fall; criticised for its indirect selection and presidential appointments.

law_name: Decree No. 188 of 2025 on official holidays
description: Set Syria's official holidays, removing Baath-era commemorations such as 8 March Revolution Day and Tishreen Liberation War Day, and adding Syrian Revolution Day on 18 March and Liberation Day on 8 December, the anniversary of Assad's fall.
significance: Replaced the Baath-era national calendar with one centred on the 2011 uprising and the 2024 change of power.

law_name: Redenomination of the Syrian pound (new banknotes)
description: Al-Sharaa and Central Bank governor Abdulkader Husrieh unveiled the new banknotes on 29 December 2025, removing zeros from the old currency; old notes were to be exchanged gradually. He said the redenomination eases transactions but 'does not itself improve the economy'. The notes began circulating in January 2026.
significance: New notes 'reflecting Syria's heritage' replaced the Assad-era issue; SANA said the change aims to simplify trade, reduce dollar dependence and restore confidence in the pound.

law_name: Decree on the rights of Syrian Kurds
description: Issued on 16 January 2026, during fighting with the SDF. It recognises Kurdish identity as part of Syria's national fabric, designates Kurdish a national language alongside Arabic that schools may teach, restores citizenship to Kurds left stateless under the Assad government and declares Nowruz a national holiday.
significance: Described by Al Jazeera as the first formal recognition of Kurdish national rights since Syria's independence in 1946; al-Sharaa has said Kurdish rights will be guaranteed by the constitution, which has not yet been drafted.

law_name: Decree No. 149 of 2026 appointing the Supreme Constitutional Court
description: Issued on 7 July 2026, appointing Issam Khaled al-Khalif as president of the Supreme Constitutional Court and six members. The court reviews the constitutionality of laws and regulations, gives opinions on draft legislation at the request of the president or the Speaker of the People's Assembly, and interprets the Constitutional Declaration.
significance: Established the constitutional court provided for in the transitional framework; all its members were appointed by the president.
